intro: The C major minuet steps straight out of the Adagio’s suspended ending. Its C minor Trio brings all four players together on one stern melody, then pulls them apart into uneasy chords.

sections.label: A · C major minuet
sections.mNote: A first-violin tune and a rising scale to finish

sections.label: B · C minor, four players together
sections.mNote: The Trio begins with a unison melody

sections.label: A′ · The C major minuet returns
sections.mNote: The da capo restores the opening dance

cues.title: Straight into the dance
cues.text: Haydn joins the Adagio to this C major minuet without a pause. After the slow movement’s wandering violin, the four players have a dance to share, marked Allegretto.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, pp. 190–191: attacca followed by Menuetto, Allegretto. Laurie Shulman discusses the connection: https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Four voices become one
cues.text: The Trio turns to C minor, the Adagio’s key. All four instruments play the same melody; tense augmented chords disturb it. The dance has acquired a grim face.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, p. 192. Shulman identifies the C minor Trio, unison melody and augmented chords. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An earlier C major quartet
cues.text: Haydn has tried this close connection between slow movement and minuet before, in the C major Quartet, Op. 20 No. 2. Here the Trio also borrows the Adagio’s C minor, so the earlier movement keeps returning inside the dance.
cues.evidence: Laurie Shulman names Op. 20 No. 2 as the precedent and describes the links between this Trio and the Adagio. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf

cues.title: Back to the minuet
cues.text: Menuetto da capo sends the quartet back to the beginning. C major returns, with the first violin leading the dance once more. Its rising scale and final chords supply the ending.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, pp. 191–192: Menuetto D.C. at the end of the Trio; the Menuetto’s rising scales and Fine.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A rising scale, then C minor
transitions.to: B · C minor, four players together
transitions.how: Rising scales carry all four instruments to the minuet’s fortissimo C major close. The Trio changes the signature to three flats and begins in C minor with all four players sharing the melody. The cello joins the tune instead of supplying a separate bass.
transitions.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, pp. 191–192; Shulman’s description of the unison C minor Trio. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf

transitions.title: The Trio hands back to the Menuetto
transitions.from: B · C minor, four players together
transitions.to: A′ · The C major minuet returns
transitions.how: The Trio ends in C minor. Menuetto D.C. sends the players straight back to the C major opening: the first violin takes the tune, and the other three resume their accompaniment. The rising scales now lead to the movement’s final stop.
transitions.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, pp. 191–192: the Trio’s close and da capo direction, returning to the Menuetto and its Fine.

quote.text: The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I.
quote.source: London notebook, after his benefit concert on 4 May 1795; our translation

composer.background:
On 4 May 1795, Haydn gave a benefit concert at the King’s Theatre in London. The programme included his new D major Symphony, now numbered 104. Afterwards he entered the result in his notebook: “The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I. I made four thousand gulden this evening. Such a thing can only be done in England.” He was sixty-three, a wheelwright’s son who had spent most of his adult life wearing an Esterházy servant’s livery.

Haydn was born in Rohrau in 1732. His father made wheels, played the harp by ear and sang; his mother had worked as a cook. At about six, Joseph left home for schooling in Hainburg. By 1740 he was a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. Singing gave him a daily education in church music, though little instruction in composition. It also gave him chances to find a meal at performances outside the cathedral. When his voice broke and he was dismissed in 1749, another musician, Johann Michael Spangler, took him into his family’s crowded room.
